opening.headline: Understand what embeddings represent in text and what similarity means.
body: There are times when I typed refund method into the search bar, but the document titled Payment Cancellation Procedure Guide does not appear. This is because the two expressions have the same meaning, but there are no overlapping words.

Embedding is a way to bridge this gap. In this lesson, we'll look at what embeddings are, how to measure how close two embeddings are, and how semantic search complements and doesn't replace keyword search.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the meaning of embedding and similarity measurement
Differences can be distinguished between similarity measurement methods.

screens.title: Documents that cannot be found because the keywords are different
screens.lead: Read queries and missed documents side by side in the search box. Think about whether the two phrases mean the same thing and why you couldn't find them.

visual.alt: A screen showing the query entered into the search box, the No Results status listed below, and the two document cards that were missed.

paragraphs: An employee entered 'refund method' into the in-house help search box. However, the result is 0. There is clearly an article in the help called 'Payment cancellation process guide'. Although they appear to be the same to a human, there are no overlapping words in the two phrases.

Keyword exact matches only check for identical words. So even if the meaning is the same, if the expression is different, it is missed. Embedding is a way to bridge this gap. Embedding turns the meaning of text into a vector of numbers, allowing you to compare whether the meaning is close rather than just the words.

OpenAI's embedding documentation explains that embeddings measure the relevance of text strings and are used for search, clustering, recommendation, anomaly detection, diversity measurement, and classification. In this class, we will cover the meaning of embedding, distance, and similarity, focusing on search.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The reason the keyword search was missed was not because there was no document, but because the wording was different. How can a computer know that the meaning is the same?

screens.outro: First, let's think about your own experience of insufficient search.

screens.title: Think about an experience where keyword search was insufficient.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think of it first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced a lack of keyword matching in text search?
items.answer: It's common to miss the document you're looking for because of synonyms, abbreviations, or other expressions. This experience shows the limitations of keyword matching, which only looks at the word's appearance and not its meaning.

items.prompt: Have you ever found a document you were looking for, but the wording was different?
items.answer: These are situations where semantic search can be helpful. Conversely, this class also shows that keyword matching works better when looking for an exact string, such as a product number.

items.prompt: How did you supplement it at that time?
items.answer: You may have supplemented your search terms by adding synonyms directly or by tagging the documents. Embedding allows us to calculate the proximity of meaning instead of this manual work.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's take a step-by-step look at what embedding is.

screens.title: What is Embedding: Meaning as Vector
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to see the step-by-step process of converting a sentence into an embedding vector and saving it.

visual.alt: A flow chart in which a sentence goes through an embedding model to become a vector, a list of numbers, and is stored in a vector store.

steps.title: Step 1: Prepare your text
steps.body: The input for embedding is text such as a sentence or paragraph. For example, the title and body of a help document can be input. Requests are charged based on the number of tokens input, so overly long posts are split appropriately.

steps.title: Step 2: Call the embedding model
steps.body: Send the text and model name to the embedding API. In OpenAI's example, we send a model name like `text-embedding-3-small`. The response contains an embedding vector and additional information.

steps.title: Step 3: The result is a list of floating point numbers
steps.body: An embedding is a list of floating point numbers, or vector. These numbers are values ​​created by a model that was trained to contain the meaning and relationships of sentences, so humans cannot read the meaning of each number. What's important is not just one number, but how the entire vector relates to other vectors.

steps.title: Step 4: The length of the vector is called the dimension.
steps.body: The number of numbers in a vector is its dimension. The default length of OpenAI is 1536 for `text-embedding-3-small` and 3072 for `text-embedding-3-large`. Larger dimensions can hold more information, but also take up more storage space.

steps.title: Level 5: Closer is more relevant
steps.body: The distance between two vectors indicates the relatedness of the two texts. If the distance is close, the relevance is high, and if the distance is far, the relevance is low. Even though the words for ‘Refund Method’ and ‘Payment Cancellation Procedure Guide’ are different, the vectors are close together.

steps.title: Step 6: Save the vector and use it for search
steps.body: The document's embedding is stored in a vector database or the like, and is compared with the query's embedding when a query comes in. This way you don't have to re-embed the document every time. Recreate document embeddings only when the document changes.

screens.outro: Now that we know what a vector is, let's look at how to measure how close two vectors are.

screens.title: Cosine Similarity and Normalization
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the description below to see a short description. Check the terms one by one.

visual.alt: Illustration showing three arrows extending from the origin in a two-dimensional plane and the angle between them.

data.text: A representative method for measuring how close two vectors are is Cosine Similarity. Cosine Similarity measures how similar the directions of two vectors are, expressed as an angle. When the directions are identical, the value is high, and when they are perpendicular, the value is zero. For example, the Cosine Similarity between two unit vectors (1, 0) and (0.8, 0.6) in a plane is 0.8, while the Cosine Similarity between (1, 0) and (0, 1) is 0. The process of normalizing vector lengths to 1 is called normalization. According to OpenAI documentation, OpenAI embeddings are normalized to length 1 via normalization, which ensures that Cosine Similarity and dot product produce the same ranking, and also results in the same ranking for Euclidean distance. Thus, the documentation recommends using Cosine Similarity while also stating that the choice of distance function is generally not critically important. However, when dimensions are directly reduced, the vector lengths are no longer 1, so normalization must be reapplied. This approach of finding documents in order of similarity is called search for meaning.

terms.tip: It is a measure of how similar the directions the two vectors are pointing are. If the directions are the same, it is close to 1, and if they are at right angles, it is 0.
This process sets the length of the vector to 1. For normalized vectors, the effect of length disappears and only the direction is compared.
This is the sum of the two vectors multiplied by their corresponding numbers. For a vector with length 1, it has the same value as cosine similarity.
The straight line distance between two vector endpoints. A vector of length 1 gives a rank equal to cosine similarity.
This is a search that finds documents based on close meaning rather than whether the words are the same. Queries and documents are embedded and sorted in order of greatest similarity.

screens.outro: Now that we know how to measure it, let’s compare cases where keyword search fails and embedding succeeds.

screens.title: Commentary: A case where keyword search fails and embedding succeeds
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the results of keyword search and embedding search for the same query. The instructor's conclusions are included in the explanation below.

states.label: Results of keyword search
states.body:
**Question**: How to get a refund?

**Results**: 0 matches as there are no matching words. Even if there is a 'Payment cancellation procedure guide' in the help, it cannot be found unless the words overlap.

**Strengths**: Strong at exact string matching. Anthropic's article explains that BM25 is particularly effective for queries containing unique identifiers or jargon. For example, when looking for 'Error code TS-999', BM25 finds exactly that string.

**Weakness**: Different expressions miss the same meaning. Vulnerable to synonyms, different word orders, and abbreviations.

**Lesson from the Case**: Just because a keyword search returns 0 results does not mean there is no document. You must first suspect that you may have missed something due to differences in expression. Even with these limitations, keyword search is still a useful tool because it is fast and the reasons for the results are clear.

states.label: Results of an embedding search
states.body:
**Question**: How to get a refund?

**Result**: When embedding the query and comparing it to the document embedding, 'Payment cancellation procedure information' comes out on top. Even if the words are different, if the meaning is close, you can find it.

**Strength**: You can find other expressions with the same meaning, sentence-level questions, and even expressions in other languages.

**Weakness**: As Anthropic writes, embedding models are good at capturing semantic relationships, but may miss items that need to be exact matches. Looking for an identifier like 'TS-999' will give you a general idea of ​​the error code and may miss the exact item.

**Instructor's Conclusion**: Semantic search complements, not replaces, exact string matching. After understanding the failures of each of the two methods, decide whether to combine them.

**Practical check**: When creating questions for evaluation, if you include questions with different expressions and questions with identifiers, you can see at a glance which method is failing and which method is failing. This result becomes the basis for deciding whether or not to combine.

screens.outro: We will summarize the main points of the lesson in the last screen.

screens.title: Embedding turns meaning into distance
screens.lead: We summarize the answer to the question posed at the beginning: how does a computer know that the meaning is the same?

paragraphs: Embedding is converting text into a numeric vector that contains meaning. If the distance between these vectors is close, the relevance is high, and if they are far, the relevance is low. So, you can find documents with the same meaning even though the words are different, such as 'How to Refund' and 'Guide to the Payment Cancellation Procedure'.

The degree of closeness is measured using a scale such as cosine similarity. Cosine similarity measures the closeness of directions, and for vectors normalized to length 1, dot product and Euclidean distance also have the same rank. If you directly reduce the dimension, you will need to normalize it again to stabilize the ranking.

Finally, remember the limitations of semantic search. Identifiers or unique terms that require an exact match may be better found by lexical matching. Closer embeddings mean they are related, not a guarantee that they are the same.

So when designing a search, we must first understand what causes our search to fail. Depending on whether it is missed due to a different expression or an identifier, it is decided whether to use semantic search or lexical matching. This judgment should be based on actual inquiries, not on intuition.

callout.label: Based on one sentence
callout.text: Embeddings turn semantics into distances, and semantic search complements exact matches.

Vocabulary matching like BM25 complements semantic search

glossary.def: This is an expression that converts text into a numeric vector containing meaning and relationships.
The number of numbers that make up the vector. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small defaults to 1536, and large defaults to 3072.
It is a measure of how similar the directions the two vectors are pointing are.
This process sets the length of the vector to 1.
This is a search that finds documents by proximity in meaning rather than by word match.

misconceptions.myth: If the embeddings are close, the exact same thing is true.
misconceptions.fact: This means that they are highly related, but does not guarantee that they are the same. Even close documents may have different contents.

misconceptions.myth: If there is a semantic search, there is no need for a keyword search.
misconceptions.fact: For items that require an exact match, such as identifiers and proper nouns, lexical matching may be more accurate. The two approaches complement each other.

misconceptions.myth: Embeddings can be mixed and compared even if the models are different.
misconceptions.fact: Since each model has a different vector space, vectors from different models should not be mixed and compared. Vectors to be compared must be made from the same model.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Embedding turns the meaning of text into numeric vectors, and measures relevance by measuring the distance between vectors.
Cosine similarity is a measure of the closeness of directions.
In normalized vectors, the ranks are stable, and directly reducing the dimensionality normalizes them again.
Semantic search complements and does not replace exact matches.
